title: A parity plot asks whether the surrogate reproduces the simulation, and whether it still does where the search goes
summary: Each dot is one parameter set: the simulation value on x, the surrogate prediction on y. If the surrogate were perfect every dot would sit on the diagonal. The figures show that for training, testing and search points the dots hug the line, and that the numbers in the legend, not the picture, tell the size of the worst miss.

media.alt: Parity plot of response-surface predictions on the y axis against direct simulations on the x axis, both from 8.0 to 9.2, with a thin diagonal line. Green squares for the training dataset and black dots for the testing dataset fall in a narrow band along the diagonal between 8.33 and 8.8. A legend gives the maximum error for each set.

source.caption: Chapter 4. Parity plot of PRS accuracy, training and testing data, ignition delay
source.note: Six Chapter 4 parity plots of a polynomial response surface against the full simulation. Two targets are shown, an ignition delay and a flame speed. For each target, one plot compares training and testing data (25, 26), one adds the points visited by a genetic-algorithm search (27, 28), and one tests the search points on a specific target (29, 30). Figures 25 to 28 label the x axis Direct simulations. Figures 29 and 30 label it Black box simulations.

read_the_figure.question: Does the polynomial surrogate reproduce the simulation on data it was trained on, on held-out data, and on the points a search visits?
read_the_figure.axes: x: the value computed by the full simulation (labelled Direct simulations, or Black box simulations in the last pair). y: the value predicted by the response surface. Both axes have equal ranges so the diagonal is at 45 degrees. Thin line: perfect agreement. Green squares: training. Black dots: testing. Red triangles: points visited by the search.
look_at: Distance of dots from the diagonal. Points on the line are perfect, above it the surrogate over-predicts, below it under-predicts.

The width of the cloud along the diagonal. The training and testing clouds span about 8.33 to 8.8 on both axes. The red triangles in figure 27 cover only a narrow sub-range in the middle, because the search converges on one region.

Outliers. In figure 29 a red triangle lies off the cloud near the low end, above the line: a search point outside the sampled range, where the surrogate extrapolates. Its legend error (0.657 percent) is more than three times the testing error (0.194 percent).
The legend numbers. Each set has a maximum error in percent. They are the quantitative summary and the picture is only a check.
Training versus testing: both clouds overlap almost perfectly, with a slightly larger maximum error for testing (0.194 against 0.116 percent), as expected.
read_the_figure.proves: That the surrogate is accurate to a fraction of a percent on the sampled domain and on the search path for these targets. It does not prove it is accurate outside the sampled range.
if_wrong: A curved cloud: the polynomial order is too low for the response.
A cloud with the right slope but offset from the diagonal: a bias, e.g. from a missing term.
A wide cloud that still hugs the diagonal at coarse scale: the plot range is wide compared with the errors, so the picture hides them.
Search points outside the training range: the surrogate extrapolates and no longer has accuracy guarantees.
must_check: Equal axis ranges and a drawn diagonal.
The quantity and unit on the axes (not given here).
The error metric in the legend is defined.
Training and testing sets are different and the testing set was not used in the fit.
The range of search points compared with the range of training points.

terms.meaning: A scatter of predicted against reference values, with the line y = x. It shows bias, scatter and range at once.
A polynomial in the parameters fitted by least squares to simulation results.
Training data are used to fit the polynomial. Testing data are held back and used only to measure accuracy.
The parameter sets visited by an optimizer, which then are evaluated by both the surrogate and the simulation as a check.
The largest relative difference between prediction and simulation on a set, in percent.
The fraction of the variance of y explained by the model.
Predicting outside the range of the training data, where a polynomial can diverge quickly.

remember: Points on the diagonal are perfect.
A parity plot over a narrow range can look excellent while hiding a few percent of error.
Use the legend number, not the picture, for the worst case.
Testing is the honest set, search points are the relevant set.
A search point outside the training range is an extrapolation.

steps.title: The fitted polynomial
steps.tex: \hat y(\mathbf x)=b_0+\sum_i b_i x_i+\sum_{i\le j}b_{ij}x_i x_j
steps.note: A full quadratic in the active parameters x. The coefficients b are found from simulation results at sampled parameter sets.

steps.title: Least squares
steps.note: The normal equations. X is the design matrix whose rows are the polynomial terms at each sample and y the simulation results. A unique solution needs enough well-spread samples.

steps.title: Parity line and residual
steps.tex: r_j=\hat y_j-y_j,\qquad r_j=0\ \text{on the line}\ \hat y=y
steps.note: The vertical distance of a dot from the diagonal is the residual. For a plot with equal axes a dot above the line is an over-prediction.

steps.title: Relative maximum error
steps.note: This is the number printed in the legends (the exact definition is inferred, not stated on the figure). It is a worst-case measure over the set.

steps.title: Why a tight cloud can hide the error
steps.note: The cloud extends about 0.47 on values of about 8.5, so a 0.2 percent error is about 0.017 in absolute terms, which is 3.5 percent of the spread of the cloud. A relative error looks small against 8.5 but not against the spread of the data.

steps.title: Explained variance
steps.note: For values spread uniformly over a span of 0.47 the standard deviation is 0.47 divided by the square root of 12, about 0.136. An rms residual of 0.005 then gives R squared of about 0.9986, a near-perfect score, even though the worst-case miss can be several times the rms. Quote the worst case as well.

worked.title: Absolute size of a legend error
worked.problem: The testing legend of figure 25 gives a maximum error of 0.194 percent, and the values are near 8.5. What is the largest absolute miss, and how big is it compared with the 0.47 span of the cloud (8.33 to 8.80)?

solution.text: Convert the percent into an absolute difference.
Divide by the span of the data.

worked.answer: The largest miss is about 0.016 in the units of the axes, about 3.5 percent of the spread of the cloud. The values 8.5, 8.33 and 8.80 are read off the axes, and the units of the axes are not stated on the figures.

analyze.q: In figure 29 the red search points scatter slightly more around the line than in figure 27, and the legend error is larger. What differs between the two plots, as far as the axis label tells you?
Why do the red triangles in figure 27 cover only a part of the diagonal while the black dots cover all of it?
analyze.hint: Where does a converged search spend its evaluations?

analyze.q: One red triangle in figure 29 lies below the low end of the black cloud. Why is its error the largest?

evaluate.q: Is a maximum error of a fraction of a percent enough to trust the surrogate to rank two candidate parameter sets that differ by less than that?
evaluate.hint: Compare the miss with the differences you want to resolve.

evaluate.q: Would you quote R squared for these plots? What would you quote instead?
evaluate.hint: Narrow range, relative error, absolute error with uncertainty.

create: Redraw the parity plot as a residual plot (residual against simulation value) with a horizontal band for the experimental uncertainty, so offsets and trends are visible at a magnified scale.
Design a plot that shows the training range as a shaded region on the x axis and marks each search point as inside or outside it.

checks.q: What does a dot on the diagonal mean?
checks.answer: The surrogate's prediction equals the simulation result for that parameter set, so there is no error at that point.

checks.q: A legend gives a maximum error of 0.194 percent for values near 8.5. What is the absolute error?
checks.answer: About 0.0165 in the units of the axes.

checks.q: Why can a parity plot look perfect while hiding a poor surrogate?
checks.hint: Scale of the axes against the scale of the errors.
checks.answer: The axes span a wide range compared with the scatter of the data, so a few percent of the data's own spread is invisible. The numbers in the legend or a residual plot show it.

checks.q: The search points lie in a small part of the training range and have a smaller maximum error than the testing set. Is that surprising?
checks.answer: No. The surrogate is best where there are many nearby samples, and the converged search spends evaluations in one region, so it can look better than a spread-out testing set.

checks.q: What would a fair test of the surrogate on the optimum look like?
checks.hint: Evaluate the surrogate and the simulation at the final parameters.
checks.answer: Run the full simulation at the optimum found with the surrogate and compare it with the surrogate's prediction there. If they agree within the target's uncertainty, the surrogate was adequate where it mattered.

provenance.notes: Standard theory only (least-squares response surface, parity plot). The legends print maximum-error percentages (0.116, 0.194, 0.170 and 0.657 percent for the ignition-delay plots), which are visible in the figures and quoted here as read from the legends. They belong to Chapter 4 of the thesis, whose uncertainty-quantification part may overlap with published work: owner to confirm they can appear. The axes carry no quantity name or unit (values between 8 and 9 look like a logarithm of ignition delay, which is an inference). The x label changes from Direct simulations to Black box simulations between plots without explanation. Figures 26, 28 and 30 were not opened individually.
